title: 1. Listening to the Ocean since 2006
text:
Overview
Ocean Networks Canada has been recording the underwater soundscape since the first installation of the VENUS node in Saanich Inlet in 2006. What started as a single location has expanded into a pan-Canadian array monitoring the Pacific, Atlantic, and Arctic coasts.
As of August 17, 2026, ONC manages 36 active hydrophones from coast to coast to coast.





Hydrophone Network at Ocean Networks Canada. Most hydrophones are located on the west coast. There is currently one in the Arctic, and one in the east coast.







Hydrophone locations in coastal BC.



This handbook is an internal source for ONC’s hydrophone network, spanning hardware specs, signal processing, and the lifecycle of an instrument.


Why listening to the ocean?
Sound is the primary way we “see” in the ocean. Because light travels poorly in water, acoustic signals are essential for navigation, communication, and monitoring the health of marine ecosystems. Unlike several oceanic instruments, hydrophones use passive acoustics, hence are a non-disruptive form of monitoring the ocean soundscape. A few applications include:

Whale monitoring to track migration patterns, distribution, abundance, and understand behaviours.
Ship traffic monitoring to identify areas of increase activity such as the Arctic in the recent years as sea ice melt unveils new shipping routes.
National defense: SOSUS (sound surveillance system) to identify vessels and nuclear testing
Resource exploration
Seismic Survey to map minerals and detect earthquakes.







Artistic view of a hydrophone under water.







Goals and future direction for passive acoustics

Delivering science-ready and trusted hydrophone data and data products
Becoming a reference in terms of passive acoustics data quality assessment and calibration
Becoming leaders in Arctic hydrophone array deployments



Territory Acknowledgment
We recognize that marine research in the Victoria region takes place on the traditional lands of the Lək̓ʷəŋən (Lekwungen) people, known today as the Songhees and Esquimalt Nations, as well as the Xwsepsum (Esquimalt) and W̱SÁNEĆ peoples.

title: 3. Hydrophone Life Cycle
text:
This section outlines the end-to-end journey of a hydrophone at ONC, from the initial purchase and contract to long-term data analysis. The life cycle is based on Aghaei et al. (2024), Best Practices for Managing Passive Acoustics Data at Ocean Networks Canada.
Hydrophones have been in use at ONC since 2006, totalling more than 700 TB of archived data.
The life cycle workflow ensures that data is not just collected, but are FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable). ONC commits to share and preserve data long-term.



Diagram of a Hydrophone life cycle at Ocean Networks Canada.




1. Planning and Governance
Teams involved: Science, DAQ, DSO, Engineers
Before a hydrophone is deployed in the water, the following legal and technical steps must be taken:

Data Agreements: ONC establishes legal agreements to define data ownership, usage restrictions, and attribution.
Stewardship: Data Stewards (DSO) apply standardized metadata and attributions to ensure the sensor is discoverable.
Product Definition: We identify new data products the community might need.



2. Data Collection & Signal Chain
Teams involved: DAQ, DSO, Systems, Marine Ops, Engineers

Hardware: We primarily use Ocean Sonics (HF/AF) and GeoSpectrum (from JASCO distributor) instruments, deployed as single units or four-element arrays.
Calibration (HydroCal): Instruments undergo rigorous pre-deployment and post-recovery calibration to ensure accuracy. If sensors drift, they are returned to the manufacturer.
Data Diversion: Hydrophones are “Tier 1” instruments, meaning that the data streams are subject to diversion by the Royal Canadian Navy and US Navy before reaching the ONC archive.
Data Transmission:

Acoustic Data: Transferred as raw audio (.wav or .flac).
Ancillary Data: Instrument “health” (temperature, humidity, clock drift) is transmitted without diversion to minitor device’s status (only for Ocean Sonics). Also referred to as auxiliary data.

Data Processing: Performed to generate Spectral Data (HSD) in MAT format, and Spectral Density Plots (HSDP) the raw audio files, and archived.
Data Availability: Data is made readily available (within a few minutes) to end-users through Oceans 3.0.



3. Commissioning
Teams involved: DAQ, DSO
Once a hydrophone is deployed and recording data, the commissioning of the device starts. This process is designed to catch technical issues early and ensures the data is “science-ready”.

Immediate Post-Deployment: Immediately after deployment, we confirm the instrument is able to record and send data to ONC archive. A public annotation is created in Oceans 3.0 to mark the start of the data streaming. A JIRA ticket is created which consolidates all relevant information.
1-2 Months Post-Deployment: A detailed analysis of data stream is performed, and several elements are analyzed including the presence of noise, saturation, array consistency (for 4 elements arrays), auxiliary data.

The commissioning ticket is closed once the data is confirmed found in the Hydrophone Data Viewer, accessible through ONC API, and that the data products are generated correctly.
For the complete procedure: Hydrophone Commissioning Procedure


4. Data Quality & Assurance
Teams involved: DAQ, Science, Systems
Because hydrophone data is classified as complex data (unlike scalar data), standard automated QAQC (like those for temperature or salinity) does not yet exist.

Manual Inspection: The DAQ team performs daily visual checks for issues like clipping, electronic interference, energy spikes, sensitivity drifts.
Annotations: Any unusual events or data gaps (caused by network maintenance, instrument failure, communication down) are recorded as annotations in Oceans 3.0 so researchers know why data might be missing.



5. Metadata & Standardization
Teams involved: DSO
To make our data globally compatible, we follow strict international standards:

ISO 19115: Governs our high-level metadata records
Global Catalogues: We align with IOOS, SeaDataNet and SeaVox device categories.
FAIR Principles: Ensuring every byte of data is Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable.
Device Action: Every event in a hydrophone life cycle, from deplyoment, calibrations, to recovery, is recorded as a permanent action in the database.



6. Preservation & Storage
Teams involved: Software, DSO, Systems

Primary Storage: Terabytes of data are stored locally at the University of Victoria data center.
Redundancy: A complete offsite backup is maintained to prevent data loss, and also shares data processing load.



7. Access & Analysis
Teams involved: Science, DSO, Software, End-Users

Discovery: Users find data via Oceans 3.0 using Data Search, the Hydrophone Viewer (5-minute spectrogram previews), or the API.
Identification: Each dataset is assigned a DOI (Digital Object Identifier) to ensure researchers can cite the specific data they used in their papers.



8. Recovery & Decommissioning
Teams involved: DSO, Marine Ops, Systems
The end of a deployement does not mean the end of a instrument’s use. Hydrophones are often re-deployed during the ONC maintenance cruises, or returning to MTC of the manufacturer for maintenance.

Post-Recovery Calibration: Once a hydrophone is pulled out of the water, calibration is performed to check if sensitivity shifted dramatically while underwater. If the before and after are very different, the instrument is often sent back to the manufacturer.
Re-Deployment: Hydrophones are often re-deployed at the same location, or at a new site. If moved to a different site, the instrument keeps its device code, but the device id will be re-assigned.
Permanent Decommissioning (Goodbye): When an instrument reaches the end of its functional life or can no longer be repaired, it is officially decommissioned in the database.

title: 4. How do Hydrophones Work?
text:
Signal to Noise ratio
Signal to Noise ratio is an important element to consider for hydrophones.
A bigger element increases sensitivity, but also can lower SNR.
A rule of thumb is to ensure the measured amplitude is at least 5 times larger than the noise equavalent pressure (NEP) of the hydrophone to maximize the signal to noise ratio (SNR).
\[
NEP [Pa] = \frac{\text{Pre-amp Noise} ~[\mu V]}{\text{Sensitivity} ~[nV~Pa^{-1}] \times \text{Pre-amp Gain}} \times 1000
\]



Signal to noise ratio measures the desired signal against the background noises. Source: hollyland

title: 5. Sound in the Ocean
text:
What is sound?
For deeper dive into the physics of sound, visit DOSITS: Science of Sound.
In the ocean, light attenuates within tens of metres, while sound can travel thousands of kilometres. That is why marine mammals and underwater systems use sound as their primary sense for communication and navigation.
Sound is created by a vibrating object. Compression and expansion produce a pressure difference, which launches a longitudinal wave: particle motion is parallel to the direction of travel. Underwater, that motion is a small back-and-forth of water molecules; the tighter the molecular bonds, the faster the energy is passed along. A sound wave is omnidirectional: it spreads in all directions.
Measurable properties:
\[
p(t) = A \sin{(2\pi f t + \phi)}
\]

title: 5. Sound in the Ocean
section: Why sound is faster in water than in air
text:
Why sound is faster in water than in air
Sound travels about 4.3 times faster in water than in air (\(\approx 1500\) m/s vs \(340\) m/s). Speed is set by bulk modulus \(B\) (stiffness) and density \(\rho\):


Bulk modulus: resistance to compression, \(B=\rho \,\partial P / \partial \rho\).
\[
v = \sqrt{B/\rho}
\]
Water is about 800 times denser than air, but about 20,000 times less compressible. That stiffness wins: energy transfers more efficiently between molecules, so sound is faster underwater.

title: 5. Sound in the Ocean
text:
SOFAR channel
Around 1000 m in the deep ocean, the decrease of temperature and the increase of pressure produce a minimum in sound speed: the SOFAR channel (SOund Fixing And Ranging). Sound always bends toward slower speed (refraction; Snell’s law). Rays that leave this layer upward or downward are refracted back into it, so energy is trapped and can travel basin-scale distances.


SOFAR channel: the depth of minimum sound speed, typically near 1000 m in mid-latitudes.

Low-frequency whale calls use this channel for long-range communication. In WWII it was used to locate downed aviators from small explosions set off in the channel.

title: 5. Sound in the Ocean
text:
Surface duct
A surface duct traps sound in the mixed layer, typically the upper tens of metres. When sound speed increases with depth just below the surface, rays refract upward, reflect from the sea surface, and stay in that shallow layer (the opposite geometry of SOFAR). Ducts are common in wind-mixed coastal waters and fade when the surface warms and stratifies.



Model simulation of sound trapped in a surface duct. Figure from Lynch et al., 2018; Fig. 5.

title: 8. ONC Hydrophone Network
text:
Ocean Networks Canada operates a massive spatial array of underwater acoustics monitoring across the country. Each hydrophone has a designated Device Code (ex: ICLISTENHF6016) and is located at a designated Location code (ex: CSQH.H1). The Location Code is used by the database, but they also have a Colloquial Name (ex: Clayoquot Slope). In addition, there are two observatories VENUS and NEPTUNE, which regroup several sites.
Most locations have a single hydrophone, while some sites have hydrophone arrays, which constitutes several hydrophones mounted together on a platform. The hydrophone arrays naming convention has .H1, .H2, etc., added to the location code, to denote the position of the hydrophone within the array.

Main locations

Pacific: NEPTUNE (offshore) and VENUS (coastal) observatories.
Arctic: Cambridge Bay, Gascoyne Inlet, NU.
Atlantic: Conception Bay, Holyrood, NL.

title: 9. Hydrophone Array Design
text:
Challenges
When mounting hydrophones, the scientific goals of ocean monitoring will dictate how the infrasctructure is built. There exists several ways that hydrophones can be arranged depending on the application. For example, while a single hydrophone can capture sound, several hydrophones together can provide direction, range, and help with separation of overlapping noises.
At Ocean Networks Canada, we use two types of arrays:
The ultimate goal for acoustics data collection is to capture high-quality soundscape while reducing unwanted noise (high Signal to Noise ratio). Noise can originate from nearby instruments, cable vibration, debris hitting the sensor, or even strong ocean currents.
While it is no small feat (or rather impossible) to eliminate noise entirely, careful infrastructure design, engineering, and testing can drastically improve data quality. In addition, we always want to minimize the risk of damage to the instrument. This section touches on all these elements.

title: 9. Hydrophone Array Design
section: Hydrophones can be deployed in several configurations:
text:
Hydrophones can be deployed in several configurations:

Single Hydrophone: Baseline monitoring.
Line Arrays: Arranged in a straight line for vertical profiling.
USBL (Ultra-Short Base Line): Used for precise underwater positioning.
SBL (Short Baseline): Examples include 3-element horizontal arrays, 4-element tetrahedral arrays, or 4-element box-type arrays.
LBL (Long Base Line): Used for tracking over wide areas.

title: 9. Hydrophone Array Design
text:
Interference
When adding hydrophones to a multi-instrument platform, all nearby infrastructure should ideally be evaluated for noise, although this is a hardeous task and we generally know after the facts if there is interference and to what internsity. Proximity interference will show up clearly as persistent lines or bursts in the spectrogram.
In this example from 2023, interference noise from instruments on the same platform at the Holyrood site was intense enough to fully mask natural ambient sound, biological vocalizations, and other signals of scientific interests.



Example of instrument interference (also referred to as noise contamination) at Holyrood, Conception Bay, NL.


After the 2023 Holyrood recordings, ONC ran a dedicated interference investigation (Holyrood Acoustic Testing Summary, Brendan Smith) to find which platform instruments were contaminating the hydrophone. The likely sources were the ADCP, the pCO₂ sensor, and the SeaBird Microcat. That work is the template for later sites: identify the noisy neighbour, then increase separation or change the duty cycle before the next deployment.
In general, in order to prevent acoustic contamination, the following “Rules of Thumb” separation distances between the hydrophone array and the systems:

Small Pumps (e.g., CTD pump): > 100 m
Large Pumps: > 2 km
Mooring chains > 5 km
Shackles/Hardware > 500 m
Active acoustics (e.g., ADCP) > 3 x the local water depth

Diagnosing interference before deployment: Acoustic modelling software (e.g., BELLHOP) can help diagnose potential interference if you know the source level, radiated frequencies, beam pattern, and beamwidth of neighboring instruments.

title: 9. Hydrophone Array Design
text:
Infrastructure and flow noise
How a hydrophone is physically attached to the infrastructure makes a massive difference in data quality. Things like loose parts, rigid attachments, or using the wrong ties may affect data quality and show up as interference, or completely mask the data. Protective mounting hardwares are designed to minimize structural interference and flow noise.
Because hydrophones are pressure sensors, they are susceptible to pressure waves generated by surface swells (which decay exponentially with depth). Wave pressure can easily saturate the hydrophone’s dynamic range. Hydrophones should generally be moored at least 20 meters deep, and significantly deeper in areas known for large swells (e.g., Folger Passage).
Here is a list of mounting material and their advantages or disadvantages:

Shock Cord/Bungee: Excellent (decouples vibration)
O-rings: Good (provides some dampening)
Rubber in a plastic clamp: Poor (transfers some vibration)
Rubber in a tight metal clamp: Bad (transfers heavy vibration)


Hydrophone guards
Hydrophones are often protected by a cage (guard or shroud), a semi-rigid housing that surrounds the hydrophone. The main purpose to prevent debris, sea life, or cables from striking the sensor. It can also help break turbulent flow (see Karman vortices) around the sensor, which can create low-frequency noise in the data.



Hydrophone guards prevent debris, sea life, and more, from hitting the sensor.


Those guards are acoustically transparent, designed so that they don’t reflect the sound waves.
In high sediments areas, platform parts can become covered by sediments which leads to corrosion and wear. Guards can prevent sediments to accumulate on hydrophone.

title: 9. Hydrophone Array Design
text:
Biofouling
Biofouling is when marine life accumulates on the instrument. This can degrade the materials or significantly reduce data quality.
The “sock method”: we use a simple sock (graciously made by a local seamstress), which is a soft and flexible cover that fit snug over the hydrophone shroud. It greatly extends lifetime of all hydrophones by preventing microorganisms to directly attach on the sensor. It can also prevent fine sediments (e.g., silt) from settling into the small gaps.



The sock method helps to prevent biofouling.


While no method is absolutely full proof, the sock-method has shown to be great success. Biofouling shows up in the data as sa slow decay of sensitivity over time.

TipExpand to learn more about the method





A spectrogram is built from short Fourier transforms of the audio:

Time windowing: raw audio is split into finite segments with a window (ONC uses a Hann window) to limit spectral leakage.
FFT: each segment is transformed from the time domain to the frequency domain.
Overlap / averaging: successive windows overlap (typically 50%) so energy at the edges is not lost.
Calibration: values are converted to micropascals with the device-specific frequency-dependent calibration curve. Using the wrong curve has caused errors in the past (internal note).

Fourier transforms assume an infinite, stationary signal. A finite cut creates edge discontinuities and spectral leakage into neighbouring bins. Windowing (tapering) multiplies the segment by a shape that goes to zero at the edges; that multiplication is a convolution, so the spectrum is the product of the signal transform and the window transform.
Choosing the right window is not easy due to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle: you cannot have perfect time and frequency resolution at once.

Narrow window: good time resolution (when a click happened), poor frequency resolution.
Wide window: good frequency resolution (harmonics of a call), poor time resolution.
Wavelengths longer than the window are lost.

ONC spectrogram settings in the example above:

Hann window with 50% overlap
6400 samples per FFT window
Temporal resolution: 0.05 s
Sample rate: 64000 Hz

HSPD is a statistical view of long-term ambient noise, originally proposed by Merchant et al. (2013). It counts how often a given dB level occurs in each frequency bin. Use it to see the persistent noise floor rather than a single 5-minute snapshot.

The mean square value in frequency range \((f, \Delta f)\) is:
\[
\Psi^2_x(f,\Delta f) = \lim_{T\rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T x(t,f,\Delta f)^2 dt
\]
Power spectral density is approximately \(\Psi^2_x(f,\Delta f) \approx G_x(f) \Delta f\):
\[
G_x(f) = \lim_{\Delta f \rightarrow 0} \frac{\Psi^2_x(f,\Delta f)}{\Delta f} = \lim_{\Delta f\rightarrow 0} \frac{1}{\Delta f} \left[ \lim_{T\rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T x(t,f,\Delta f)^2 dt \right]
\]
HSPD then histograms those levels per frequency bin over a long window, so the colour is occupancy (how often that level occurs), not a single spectrogram frame.

title: 13. Data Diversion
text:
Tier 1 Instruments
Underwater acoustics data may reveal sensitive information that poses national security concerns. Hydrophones, alongside Accelerometers, Seismometers, Tiltmeters, and Magnetometers, are classified as Tier 1 instruments.
Therefore, the passive acoustic data stream may be re-routed through a Data Diversion System (DDS) controlled by the Royal Canadian Navy (RCN) and US Navy (USN) to screen for sensitive maritime activity. These divert periods can range from minutes to days or even weeks.
During diversion, full-band audio files (WAV/FLAC) are diverted directly to naval screening facilities, and the data is released back later to ONC either untouched, high-passed-filtered (HPF), or low-passed-filtered (LPF). “HPF-” and “LPF-” suffixes are then incorporated into the file name (ex: ICLISTENHF6016_20250317T000500.000Z-LPF.flac).



Example of Low-Passed-Filtered spectrogram at Clayoquot Slope. Notice the file header “Data Diversion Mode”.


Notifications regarding planned or active diversions are managed via a restricted mailing list reserved strictly for cleared personnel.

title: 14. Science and Publications
text:
Marine mammals monitoring
Underwater sound monitoring is used at ONC for monitoring whale activity and behavior. In 2015, ONC joined the Enhancing Cetacean and Habitat Observation (ECHO) Program which aim at investigating ways to reduce shipping traffic impacts on whale activity in the Straight of Georgia. As part of the program, hydrophone arrays from JASCO Applied Science were deployed and the data ingested in ONC’s servers.
The program has known quite a bit of success, as thousands of ships have voluntarily reduced speed or distanced themselves from whales.
Read ONC’s story here.
Since then, ONC has kept expanding its hydrophone network which has turned into more partnerships with BC in 2017, to study ship traffic in Haro Strait (read story here to specifically monitor southern residents killer whales.
Whale monitoring is continuously undergoing, thanks to in-house bio acoustician Lynn Rannankari, who helps identify species as well as differentiate different calls that a single species makes and relates to their behavior, and their seasonal presence.

title: 14. Science and Publications
text:
Fin whale autodetector
Historically, whale identification in hydrophone data is done by listening to the audio file. This method, while proof, is extremely time-consuming. At ONC, Spencer Bialek has developed a Machine Learning tool able to detect several whale species and differentiate several calls. The first iteration of this model was applied to fin whales, which are extremely common in BC and we have tons of recordings. The model is able to identify 3 distinct call types: 20 Hz, 40 Hz, and song. Each of these are associated with different behaviors such as mating, grazing, communication and navigation (read more about fin whales on DOSIT).
The model is able to do in a few minutes what humans typically would do in several weeks or months, which allows for building long-term time series of whale presence. However, humans are needed to guide the model, detect false alarms (misidentified whale call), and inject more data. Moreover, the model is not able to detect new call types which humans are able to detect. Humans will always be needed together with this model, but so far it is bringing a lot of hopes analyzing terabytes of audio files.

title: 14. Science and Publications
text:
Acoustic modelling
Hydrophones record the soundscape; modelling asks how the environment shapes that sound. Temperature, depth, seamounts, and seafloor sediments control how far a call travels, and therefore the detection range of a hydrophone. That range depends on frequency — and so on species and call type — with lower frequencies travelling farther. Modelling is used to place new instruments outside deaf zones. The underlying physics is in Sound in the Ocean.
Lanfranco Muzi, underwater acoustician at ONC, has used acoustic modelling to characterize soundscape changes during COVID, when shipping was significantly reduced.

title: 14. Science and Publications
text:
Earthquake detection
Seismic waves from earthquakes travel with typical frequencies between 5-50 Hz, making them detectable on low-frequency hydrophones which have high sensitivity down to 10 Hz. However, hydrophones are not the primary sensors used for earthquake detection, since ONC has several Ocean-Bottom seismometers (OBS).
Interesting to note that conversely, seismometers can also be used to detect whale calls. OBS have been deployed around Endeavour hydrothermal vent, starting with eight in early 2000s and more since then. Fin whale calls are relatively low frequency (20 Hz), and overlap with the detection bandwidth of these seismometers. Numerous studies have used them to track fin whales (Weirathmueller et al., 2007,Wilcock 2012, Soule & Wilcock, 2013).

title: 15. Useful Equations
text: Speed of Sound in Seawater

title: 15. Useful Equations
text:
Mackenzie, 1981
A nine-term fit, convenient for a first estimate of \(c\) from a CTD cast:
\[
c(T,S,z) = a_1 + a_2 T + a_3 T^2 + a_4 T^3 + a_5(S-35) + a_6 z + a_7 z^2 + a_8 T (S-35) + a_9 T z^3
\]
where \(T\) is temperature (°C), \(S\) is salinity (psu), \(z\) is depth (m), and \(c\) is sound speed (m/s). Coefficients \(a_1 \ldots a_9\) are given in Mackenzie (1981). Typical range of validity: \(T\) 0–30 °C, \(S\) 30–40 psu, \(z\) 0–8000 m.

title: 15. Useful Equations
text:
Del Grosso, 1974
Often preferred when a more accurate oceanographic sound speed is needed. It is a function of temperature, salinity, and pressure:
\[
c(T,S,p) = c_{000} + \Delta c_T + \Delta c_S + \Delta c_P + \Delta c_{STp}
\]
where \(c_{000}\) is a reference sound speed and the \(\Delta c\) terms are polynomial corrections for temperature, salinity, pressure, and their cross terms. Full coefficients are given in Del Grosso (1974).

title: 17. Glossary
section: Definition of acousitc metrics and terms
text:
Definition of acousitc metrics and terms

Absorption
Reduction of acoustic pressure amplitude due to acoustic particle motion energy converting to heat in the propagation medium.


Ambiant sound/noise
Sound that would be present in the absence of a specified activity. It is location-specific and time-specific. def 2: all-encompassing sound at a given place, usually a composite of sound from many sources near and far (e.g. shipping vessels, seismic activity, precipitation, sea ice, wave, biological activity).


Attenuation
Gradual loss of acoustic energy from absorption and scattering as sound propagates through a medium.


Background noise
All sound recorded by the hydrophone in the absence of the pile driving signal for a specified pile driving acoustic signal beaing measured. ### Propagation loss


Cetacean
Any anumal in the order Cetacea. These are aquatic, mostly maine mammals and include whales, dolphins, and porpoises.


Compressional wave
A mechanical vibration wave in which the direction of particle motion is parallel to the direction of the propagation. Also called primary wave, or P-wave.


Decibel (dB)
Relative unit of measurement equal to one-tenth of a bel, measuring the level when the base of the logarithm is the tenth root of ten, and the quantities concerned are proportional to power.


Ensonified
Exposed to sound.


Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)
A computationally efficiently algorithm for computing the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT). A DFT requires \(O(n^2)\) computations, while an FFT requires \(O(n log n)\). A Fourier transform converts a signal from its original domain (time/space) to a representation in the frequency domain.


Frequency
The rate of oscillation of a periodic function measured in cycles-per-unit-time. Symbol: \(f\). Unit: Hertz (Hz), is equal to 1 cycle per second.


Intensity
The intensity (\(I\)) of a sound wave is defined as the energy transmitted through a unit area, per unit time, in the direction in which the sound wave is traveling. It is a vector quantity having both a magnitude and direction.
\[
\vec{I} = p \vec{u}
\]
where \(p\) is pressure, and \(u\) the particle velocity.


Impedance
Impedance of water is much greater than that of air.


Power Spectrum Density
The acoustic signal power per unit frequency as measured at a single frequency. Unit: \(\micro Pa^2\cdot s\)


Pressure
Unit: Pa

acoustic: deviation from the ambient hydrostatic pressure caused by a sound wave.
hydrostatic: pressure at any given depth in a static liquid that is the result of the weight of the liquid acting on a unit area at that depth, plus any pressure acting on the surface of the liquid.



Reverberation
Sound resulting from cumulative scattering of sound by an aggregation, or ensemble, of scatterers.


Root-mean-square sound pressure level (SPL) \(L_{p,rms}\)
The Root Mean Square (RMS) of the sound pressure taken over a time interval \(\Delta t = t_2-t_1\) [s]. Starting from the Mean Square average sound pressure \(p_{ms}\), [Pa$^2] the RMS pressure \(p_{rms}\) [Pa] is:
\[
p_{ms} = \bar p^2 = \frac{1}{\Delta t} \int_{t_1}^{t_2} p^2 (t) dt
\]
… there is more…


Soundscape
Underwater acoustics characterization of the ambient sound in terms of its spatial, temporal and frequency attributes, and the types of sources contributing to the sound field. ### Pulse duration The pulse duration is the percentage energy signal duration over the acoustic pulse, defined in ISO 18406, assuming an energy percentage for the pulse duration of 90%.


Sound pressure (\(p\))
Contribution to total pressure caused by the action of sound. Sound pressure is a function of time: \(p=p(t)\), and expressed in pascals (Pa).


Sound pressure spectrum (\(P\))
Fourier transform of the sound pressure. Sound pressure spectrum is a function of frequency: \(P=P(f)\), and expressed in pascals per hertz (Pa Hz-1). The formula form is:
\[
P(f) = \int_\infty^\infty exp\left(-2\pi i f t \right) p(t) dt
\]

Sound speed profile
Speed of sound in the water column as a function of depth below the water surface.


Spectrogram
A visual representation of acoustic amplitude compared with time and frequency.
